1. The slave star rises.

In Estonian folk astronomy the brightest star of the sky, Sirius, is called the Slave Star (Orjatäht). According to tradition, in the days of serfdom the peasants were let go home from threshing at the manor when the slave star had risen.

Calculate at what time the threshing ended on St Martin's Day, 10 November. The coordinates of Sirius are $\alpha = 6^\mathrm{h}45^\mathrm{m}$, $\delta = -16^\circ43'$.

2. Evening star Venus.

Going out in the evening you will find a very bright "star" in the western sky. It is our neighbouring planet Venus, which is rapidly approaching inferior conjunction. Venus reaches conjunction with the Sun on 27 March.

Calculate how far Venus is from the Earth this evening. Also find the phase of Venus and draw how it appears in a telescope. The orbits of the Earth and Venus may be taken as circular.

3. Triton.

Neptune's satellite Triton appears to us as a star of magnitude 13.5 and observing it requires quite a good telescope. How bright would Triton appear if it orbited Mars, at a mean opposition of Mars?

Is the result plausible? Explain why! ($D_\mathrm{Mars} = 6800$ km; $D_\mathrm{Triton} = 2700$ km; $A_\mathrm{Mars} = 0.15$; $A_\mathrm{Triton} = 0.76$)

4. Collision in space.

10 February 2009 goes down in the history of astronautics: at an altitude of 776 km above the Taymyr Peninsula the Russian satellite Kosmos-2251 and the US communications satellite Iridium-33 collided. Both were completely destroyed; 500 larger and countless smaller fragments were thrown into space. It was the first real "cosmic collision" in the 52-year history of astronautics. The positions and paths of the satellites are shown on the map below.

Calculate the relative velocity of the satellites at the moment of the collision and the energy released in the collision, assuming that both moved on circular orbits. The mass of Kosmos-2251 was 900 kg, that of Iridium 690 kg.

5. Approaching star.

It is known that the star nearest to the Earth is Proxima Centauri, which is 4.243 light years from the Sun. But this star has a competitor: Barnard's Star, which is now in second place by distance, at 5.98 ly from us, is approaching us with a speed of 106.8 km/s. It will not run straight into the Sun, since its proper motion of 10.37 arcseconds per year carries it aside.

Calculate when Barnard's Star will be closest to the Sun. At what distance will it pass us?

6. Large and small Sun.

This graph – an HR diagram – shows the evolution of the Sun from its present state (on the main sequence) until it becomes a white dwarf. The axes of the graph are temperature and absolute bolometric luminosity.

Estimate the largest and the smallest diameter of the Sun during the evolution shown on the graph.

Problem 1. Mountains and clocks

The Kyrgyz Republic is an interesting country which, despite its small size, has two time zones. In most of the territory of Kyrgyzstan the time zone GMT+6 is used, but in the immediate surroundings of the city of Osh GMT+5 applies. The height of the highest mountain there, Jengish Chokusu (in translation "Victory Peak"), has repeatedly been measured wrongly, with differences of even more than a kilometre. The result now generally accepted is 7439 metres.

One fine morning the Kyrgyz Almazbek watched the sunrise from the window of his home in Osh ($40^\circ31'48''$ N, $72^\circ48'0''$ E) and noticed that the clock showed exactly 6:00. Wishing to share the beautiful sunrise time, Almazbek phoned his friend Askar in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek, so that he too could see a full-hour morning. But the phone was answered by Askar's wife, who said that Askar had gone to climb Jengish Chokusu ($42^\circ02'15''$ N, $80^\circ07'30''$ E) and was at the summit of the mountain at that very moment. Askar's wife also said that Askar uses only true solar time, because he does not like zone time. Now the questions:

1. What did a clock set to zone time show in Bishkek?

2. Did Askar see the sunrise earlier or later than Almazbek? Justify, taking into account the east–west difference in location and the fact that Askar is on the summit of the mountain.

3. Make a drawing of the effect of the mountain on the time and calculate what Askar's clock, set to solar time, showed when he saw the Sun rise. You may assume that there was no other landform in front of the horizon in the eastern direction; the ground level east of the mountain may be taken as 3000 m.

4. What was the difference between Askar's and Almazbek's clocks? That is, we ask what their clocks showed at the same moment (one in solar time, the other in zone time).

Problem 2. Let us look at the Cat's Eye

The Cat's Eye Nebula (NGC 6543) is one of the best-known planetary nebulae. Planetary nebulae arise from Sun-like stars which, at the end of their "life", when the fuel needed for thermonuclear reactions (mainly hydrogen) starts to run out, throw off their outer layers. As a result of such an explosion, rapidly receding gas layers form around these stars; an image of them and a drawing of the shells are shown in Figure 3 (the figures are in a separate appendix, and the shells appear as discs). The diameter of the Cat's Eye Nebula on the celestial sphere is about 30 arcseconds. The Hubble Space Telescope photographed the Cat's Eye Nebula twice, on 18.09.1994 and 17.08.1997 (see Figure 4). As can be seen, it is not easy to detect the motion of the gas shells from these images. Fortunately, we know that the transverse expansion velocity of the middle disc (marked E25 in the figure) along the shorter semi-axis is 16.4 km/s. We also know that the expansion rate in angular units can be expressed through the expansion velocity in physical units by the formula
$$D = \frac{v}{\omega}, \qquad (1)$$
where $D$ is the distance of the observed object, $v$ is the transverse velocity in units of length and $\omega$ is the transverse velocity in angular units.

To find the distance of the Cat's Eye Nebula, we use a technique in which we subtract the second image from the first pixel by pixel. In this way we see exactly where changes have occurred, because the structure of the gas shells stays the same. If we enlarge the first image, we can find the magnification factor ($F$) for which the two images are as similar as possible (the resulting subtracted image is called a residual image); from this one can derive the angular expansion rate of the discs of the Cat's Eye Nebula using the formula
$$\omega = \frac{(F-1)\,d}{t}, \qquad (2)$$
where $F$ is the magnification factor, $d$ is the distance of the edge of the disc from the central star (along the shorter semi-axis) measured in radians, and $t$ is the time. $d$ can be found, for example, from Figure 5. The magnification factor can be found from Figure 6 by finding the image with the least structure. If several images seem equally good, their average may be taken. Now all that remains is to find the distance of the Cat's Eye Nebula. Also find when the central star exploded, assuming that the expansion has proceeded at a constant rate.

Problem 3. Brightnesses of stars

Jaanus took a long-exposure picture of the sky, wanting to measure the brightness of the star Vega, whose brightness is by definition 0 magnitude. For this he had developed a computer program that automatically finds the brightness of a star in an image. Unfortunately, while taking the photo he did not notice that at the beginning of the exposure an aeroplane flew past in front of this star, leaving behind a trail (with optical depth $\tau = 0.02$) which dispersed in 2.5 minutes. The aeroplane's lights were 4 times brighter than the star, and the flyover lasted 2 seconds. By how many per cent did Jaanus err in measuring the brightness of the star, and did he underestimate or overestimate the brightness of the star? The total exposure time was 250 seconds.
$$I/I_0 = e^{-\tau}, \qquad (3)$$
where $I_0$ is the initial brightness and $I$ is the observed brightness.

Problem 4. "Melting" comets

As is known, comet ISON was potentially one of the brightest comets of this century that mankind could have seen, but unfortunately it disintegrated at perihelion. This was caused by the too great influence of the Sun: if a comet heats up too much, it melts away and disintegrates.

Assuming that the comet was in thermodynamic equilibrium (i.e. emission and absorption are equal), find what the surface temperature of ISON was at perihelion. The diameter of ISON may be taken as 5 km. The Stefan–Boltzmann law describes the radiative power of bodies:
$$L = \sigma_\mathrm{SB} S T^4, \qquad (4)$$
where $S$ is the surface area of the object, $\sigma_\mathrm{SB}$ the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and $T$ the temperature. It has also been found, by observing occultations of stars by comets, that the optical depth of the coma (the gas cloud surrounding the nucleus) of a comet near the nucleus is below 13.3; for this problem it may be taken as 7. At perihelion the distance of ISON from the Sun was 0.01244 au, and its albedo may be taken, for example, as 0.04. In the present formulation of the problem the answer is not quite correct; what additional assumptions need to be used to solve the problem correctly?

Constants: Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma_\mathrm{SB} = 5.67\cdot10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,K^{-4}\,m^{-2}}$; luminosity of the Sun $L_\odot = 3.839\cdot10^{26}$ W; astronomical unit 1 au $= 1.496\cdot10^{11}$ m; speed of light $c = 299\,792$ km/s.

Problem 5 – "Standard candles"

On 21 January 2014 at 19:20 GMT the English astronomer Steve Fossey, together with his students, discovered a supernova in the nearby galaxy M82. Based on the year and order of discovery it was named SN 2014J. It quickly turned out that it was a so-called standard candle, a type Ia supernova. The community of professional and amateur astronomers set about carefully observing the fresh standard candle. It was found that a couple of weeks after the discovery the supernova reached its maximum visual brightness (brightness in the V filter, see Figure 2). It was also estimated that there is quite a lot of dust between us and the supernova, and therefore SN 2014J appears to us one magnitude fainter.

Type Ia supernovae are thought to arise when, as a result of the transfer of matter onto the white dwarf in a binary system consisting of a white dwarf close to the Chandrasekhar limiting mass and an ordinary star, the critical mass limit of 1.38 solar masses is exceeded, and the white dwarf explodes as a supernova owing to the onset of carbon thermonuclear reactions.

It is already known that the maximum absolute brightness of type Ia supernovae is $M_V = -19.3^\mathrm{m}$. Estimate the distance of the galaxy M82.

Assuming that the temperature of the white dwarf before the explosion was 100 000 K, its radius equal to the radius of the Earth, and that the galaxy M82 is at a distance of 11.5 million light years, would it have been possible to observe the white dwarf that was the progenitor of SN 2014J before the explosion from the Earth with the 10-metre Keck telescope? The faintest stars observable with the Keck telescope have brightness $+30^\mathrm{m}$.

Constants: Stefan–Boltzmann constant $\sigma_\mathrm{SB} = 5.67\cdot10^{-8}\ \mathrm{W\,K^{-4}\,m^{-2}}$; luminosity of the Sun $L_\odot = 3.839\cdot10^{26}$ W; astronomical unit 1 au $= 1.496\cdot10^{11}$ m; speed of light $c = 299\,792$ km/s.

Problem 6 – "In a row"

Small aliens, the rabaraks, as the result of some strange accident ended up on Mercury. They built themselves a shuttle that travels at a speed of $0.01\,c$. In the year 45637234 of the rabaraks' calendar (the length of the year is the same as the Earth's year) all the planets of the Solar System were in one line. Then the rabaraks set off towards Neptune. For reasons arising from the rabaraks' religion, however, they were allowed to travel only from each planet to the next one at a time, i.e. from Mercury to Venus, from there to the Earth, and so on. The second religious restriction was that they were allowed to start flying only when the planets were in opposition to each other. Did the rabaraks reach Neptune within 200 years? If yes, in what year (according to the rabaraks' calendar); if not, how far did they get?

Problem 1. Have people been on the surface of the Moon?

Nowadays conspiracy theories about people having been on the Moon are very popular. According to the conspiracy theorists, their claims could be refuted by photographing the base platforms of the lunar modules still on the Moon, for example with the Hubble Space Telescope. Is it possible to photograph the descent modules of Apollo 11, 12, 14–17 on the Moon with the Hubble Space Telescope? And the US flags on the Moon? Justify your answer with calculations.

Some data about the Hubble Space Telescope:

Altitude above the Earth's surface: 555 km

Diameter of the primary mirror: 2.4 metres

Focal length: 57.6 metres

Launch date: 25 April 1990.

The dimensions of the lunar module seen from above are $5.5 \times 4.3$ metres.

Problem 2. Wandering stars

One of the main problems of ancient astronomy was explaining the apparent paths of the planets in the sky. The final solution was given by Kepler with his three laws:

1. The orbits of the planets are ellipses, and the Sun is at one focus of their orbits.

2. In equal time intervals the planets sweep out sectors of equal area (the corners of the sector: Sun – planet at time 1 – planet at time 2).

3. The quotient of the square of the period and the cube of the semi-major axis is a constant.

He found these laws by studying the orbit of Mars, above all its retrograde motion during a certain period. What is it caused by? Today the periods of the Earth and Mars are known, (365.24, 686.97) days, the semi-major axes (1.0, 1.5237) au, and the orbital eccentricities $e = \sqrt{1-(b/a)^2}$ are 0.0167 and 0.0934 ($a$ and $b$ are the short and the long semi-axis respectively). Find the maximum retrograde speed of Mars in the visible sky. You may assume that the orbits lie in the same plane and that for the Earth and Mars the semi-major axis is approximately equal to the mean distance from the Sun. You may not assume constant speeds of the planets or a constant orbital radius.

Problem 3. Planets in a row

In the spring of 2011 one could see in the morning how almost all the planets were located on one line, see Figure 1. Make a plan of the Solar System showing how they are located in space (the diagram must show the Sun, the orbits of all the planets and their positions on the orbits). Find which planet is closest to the Earth and which planets are farthest from each other. Give the answers in astronomical units.

Problem 4. Curiosity on Mars

The newest Mars rover, Curiosity, is carrying out various rock analyses on Mars. At present it is driving somewhere near Mount Sharp. At 14:22:37 NASA scientists noticed that $30$ degrees to the right of the rover's direction of travel, at a distance of 300 m, there is a rock formation promising for mass spectrometry. In exactly five minutes the scientists made the necessary calculations to set Curiosity's direction of travel towards the formation and sent the course-change command to the rover. Estimate in which direction the rover must turn (without knowing the exact positions of the planets) and when it will reach the rock formation, taking the rover's driving speed to be 4 km/h all the time. You may assume that communication takes place at the speed of light and that the rover turns instantaneously.

Problem 1. Supernova

In 1604 Kepler's supernova was visible in the sky; it is the most recent supernova seen with the naked eye. Its apparent magnitude is estimated to have been $m_S = -2.5$, and it was at a distance of 5 kpc. How many Suns would have to be placed at the same distance ($d = 5$ kpc) right next to each other so that the Suns together would appear as bright as Kepler's supernova?

Problem 2. Calculate like Copernicus (10 points)

One day Jupiter and the Earth were in opposition (the Sun, the Earth and Jupiter were aligned on one line). 87.5 days later the Earth and Jupiter were in quadrature, i.e. the Earth, the Sun and Jupiter formed a right angle. 311.5 days later Jupiter is again in opposition. You know that the sidereal period of the Earth is 365.2425 days. While solving this problem you do not know Kepler's laws or the masses of the planets. Find:

1. What is the synodic period of Jupiter (the relative position Sun–Earth–Jupiter is the same)?

2. Find the sidereal period of Jupiter.

3. Calculate the distance of Jupiter (in astronomical units), using only the quantities given in the problem.

Problem 3. Redshift (10 points)

We see cosmic objects thanks to atoms and molecules which, in large numbers, send light towards us at definite wavelengths. In 1929 Edwin Hubble discovered that most galaxies appear redder than they should, assuming that they consist mainly of hydrogen like our galaxy. This led to the discovery of the expansion of the Universe. The expansion of the Universe is measured by the Hubble constant and denoted $H_0$.

The redshift of galaxies is usually measured by the quantity $z$. Suppose you observe a galaxy with $z = 0.3$, knowing that the spectrum of the hydrogen H$\alpha$ line has wavelength 486.1 nm, and assuming that the Doppler shift approximation $z \approx \frac{v}{c}$ holds. Then:

1. At what wavelength do we see this galaxy?

2. How far into the past do we see when looking at this galaxy?

In the binary system 2MASS J05215658+4359220 there is one of the smallest black holes currently known; the other component of the system appears to be a giant star. The eccentricity of the orbits of the system is 0.005, and the mass of the star has been estimated at approximately $3.2\,M_\odot$. Assume that the orbital plane of the system is approximately parallel to our line of sight. Find the mass of the black hole (in solar masses) and its Schwarzschild radius.

Problem 5. Eclipse (30 points)

Tomorrow, 8 April, a total solar eclipse will be visible in North America; its path is shown on the map. Estimate the total duration of the solar eclipse on the Earth in hours and minutes (i.e. the time during which the Moon's umbra exists at some point of the Earth). Also estimate how fast (m/s) the umbra moves for an observer on the Earth's surface at the point of greatest eclipse. It is known that the point of greatest eclipse (the point where the altitude of the Sun above the horizon during the eclipse is greatest) is in Mexico; its latitude is $\varphi = 25^\circ$ N and the altitude of the Sun above the horizon is $h = 70^\circ$.

As a simplification, you may assume that the eclipse takes place approximately at the vernal equinox and that the inclination of the Moon's orbit to the Earth's orbit is negligible.

Problem 6. A universe without dark energy (30 points)

(i) Find the relation between redshift and temperature. It should take the form $T = T_0(1+z)^x$, where $x$ is a constant that you must find and $T_0 \approx 2.7$ K is the temperature of the Universe today (please also write the derivation, not only the final answer). Hint: Wien's displacement law may be useful.

(ii) Recombination is the epoch, nearly 380 000 years after the Big Bang, when electrons and protons formed neutral hydrogen atoms for the first time. It took place at redshift $z \approx 1100$. Find the temperature of the Universe at the moment of recombination.

The Friedmann equation can be given in the form
$$\left(\frac{\dot a(t)}{a(t)}\right)^2 = H_0^2\left(\frac{\Omega_{r,0}}{(a(t))^4} + \frac{\Omega_{m,0}}{(a(t))^3} + \Omega_{\Lambda,0} + \frac{\Omega_\kappa}{(a(t))^2}\right),$$
where $a$ is the dimensionless scale factor, which describes the expansion of the Universe, and $\dot a(t) = \frac{da(t)}{dt}$ thus describes the rate of expansion of the Universe. $H_0$ is the Hubble constant today and $\Omega_0$ are the density parameters of the Universe today (the index $m$ denotes matter, $r$ radiation, $\Lambda$ dark energy and $\kappa$ curvature). Also, today $a(t=0) = a_0 = 1$.

(iii) If the Hubble constant today is $H_0 = \left.\frac{\dot a(t)}{a(t)}\right|_{a_0}$, how are the density parameters related to each other?

(iv) Assume that the Universe is flat ($\kappa = 0$) and that in the present Universe $\Omega_{r,0} \approx 0$. Write the Friedmann equation if the Universe also had no dark energy.

(v) Put the equation obtained in part (iv) into the form $\dot a(t) = C(a(t))^k$, where $C$ and $k$ are numerical constants. Solve this equation, i.e. find $a(t)$ and eliminate $\dot a(t)$. Hint: if a differential equation is given in the form $\dot a(t) = C(a(t))^k$ and $C$ and $k \neq 0, -1$ are constants, then (in the context of this problem!) the relation between $a(t)$ and $t$ is $\frac{a^{1-k}}{1-k} = Ct$, if at the moment of the Big Bang $t = 0$ and $a = 0$.

(vi) Find the age of this universe. Is it consistent with observational data? Justify.

(vii) Assuming that recombination in this universe still took place at redshift $z = 1100$, how many years after the Big Bang should it have taken place?

(viii) Describe briefly what the further fate of this universe is.

Problem 2. Birth of a galaxy (10 points)

When a galaxy forms, it changes its state from a simply gravitationally bound state $E_\mathrm{kin} = |E_\mathrm{pot}|$ to the virial state $E_\mathrm{kin} = 0.5\cdot|E_\mathrm{pot}|$. The excess binding energy is radiated away. Let us study the formation of an idealised disc galaxy which rotates uniformly with speed $v_\mathrm{rot} = 250$ km/s; we may ignore all random motions, inhomogeneities of the mass distribution, etc. Suppose that all its mass lies within $R_\mathrm{max} = 80$ kpc. Suppose that it formed in 600 million years. With what luminosity (in units of the solar luminosity) does this galaxy radiate during this time owing to the release of the binding energy?

Problem 4. Exomoon (15 points)

The formulation of the problem partly follows the approach of Kipping (2009) (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2966.2008.13999.x) to the topic.

TTVs (transit timing variations) are periodic changes in the timing of the observed mid-point of the transit of an exoplanet. They may be caused, for example, by an exomoon or by another planet of the system which, through gravity, periodically "perturbs" the orbit of the observed planet around the star.

If the planet has an exomoon, the photometric mid-point of the transit of this planet ($t$) does not coincide with the moment when the centre of mass of the planet–moon system is at the mid-point of the transit ($t_0$).

If there are no TTVs, the observed mid-point of the transit and the "physical" mid-point occur at the same moment.

If $\mathrm{TTV} \equiv t - t_0 > 0$, the transit was late; if $\mathrm{TTV} = t - t_0 < 0$, we saw the transit too early.

Next we study how measuring the TTV values of an exoplanet helps us to describe the exomoon orbiting it. For simplicity, assume that all the orbits are approximately circular ($e \approx 0$) and that the orbital planes of both the planet–moon and the planet–star systems are parallel to our line of sight.

(a) (13 p) Show that $\Delta\mathrm{TTV} \equiv \max(\mathrm{TTV}) - \min(\mathrm{TTV})$ is
$$\Delta\mathrm{TTV} = \frac{1}{\pi}\sqrt[3]{P_m^2 P_p \frac{m^3}{M_p^2 M_\star}}, \qquad (1)$$
where $P_m$ is the sidereal period of the moon around the planet, $P_p$ is the period of the planet around the star, $m$ is the mass of the moon, $M_p$ is the mass of the planet and $M_\star$ is the mass of the star. You may assume that $m \ll M_p$, $M_p \ll M_\star$ and that the duration of the transit is much shorter than the orbital period of the moon around the planet.

(b) (2 p) Calculate the theoretical value of $\Delta\mathrm{TTV}$ for the Earth–Moon system.

The SNR (signal-to-noise ratio) shows the quality of observationally collected data and measures how much stronger the "signal" of our object of observation (for example a galaxy or the transit of an exoplanet) is than the background noise.

Assume that for one observation (data collected during one exposure time) the estimated SNR of the star is
$$\mathrm{SNR}_\star = \sqrt{A\,\Delta t\int q(\lambda)F(\lambda)\,d\lambda} \approx \sqrt{qAF_0\,\Delta t\,\Delta\lambda\cdot10^{-0.4m}}. \qquad (2)$$
$q$ is the quantum efficiency of the instrument, $A$ the area of the primary mirror of the telescope, $\Delta t$ the exposure time, and $\Delta\lambda$ the width of the observed wavelength range. $F_0$ is the mean energy flux of Vega, given as the number of incoming photons divided by unit time, unit area and unit wavelength. Problem 7. Lambert sphere (30 points)

The phase curves of planets describe how the brightness of a planet changes in time, depending on its orbit and on the viewing angle relative to the observer. One of the simplest and most widely used models for analysing phase curves is the Lambert sphere model, which assumes that the surface of the planet reflects light diffusely and isotropically.

In the Lambert sphere model the phase curve is found by the following formula:
$$\Phi(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\pi}\left[\sin\alpha + (\pi-\alpha)\cos\alpha\right]$$
where:

$\alpha$ is the phase angle, i.e. the angle between the star, the planet and the observation ($0^\circ$ means full phase, $180^\circ$ means new phase),

$\Phi(\alpha)$ is the apparent relative brightness compared with full phase.

(a) Calculate the values of the phase function $\Phi(\alpha)$ for the following phase angles:
$$\alpha = 0^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 90^\circ,\ 120^\circ,\ 180^\circ.$$
Round the results to three decimal places. (5 points)

(b) The ratio of the fluxes of the planet and the star for a Lambert sphere is the following:
$$\frac{F_\text{planet}}{F_\text{star}} = A_g\cdot\frac{R_\text{planet}^2}{a^2}\cdot\Phi(\alpha) \qquad (3)$$
where:

$A_g$ is the geometric albedo of the planet,

$R_p$ is the radius of the planet compared with full phase,

$a$ is the distance between the planet and the star.

Suppose that the geometric albedo of the Lambert sphere at 500–800 nm is 0.2, the radius of the planet is equal to the radius of the Earth and the distance of the planet from the star is equal to the distance of the Earth from the Sun.

1) Calculate and draw as a graph the planet–star flux $F_\text{planet}$ in the range $\alpha = 0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$.

2) Mark the maximum and minimum values on the graph.

(10 points)

(c) How does the formula of the phase curve of the Lambert sphere depend on the inclination of the orbit? (5 points)

(d) Show that the phase curve $\Phi(\alpha)$ reaches its maximum at the point $\alpha = 0$ in the interval $\alpha = [0,\pi]$.

Derive the first derivative $\frac{d\Phi}{d\alpha}$ of $\Phi(\alpha)$.

Check that $\frac{d\Phi}{d\alpha} < 0$ for all values $\alpha > 0$ in the interval $\alpha = [0,\pi]$.
